en: When the night of Brahmā had passed and the Lotus-born One had awakened,
Viṣṇu, desiring to create living beings, perceived that the earth was submerged by the waters.
Just as in former kalpas, he who delights in auspicious water-sports assumed the form of a boar and lifted up the earth.
The Vedas are his feet, the sacrificial posts his tusks, the rituals his teeth, and the fire-altars his mouth;
Agni is his tongue, the Darbha grass his hair, and the Veda his head—he of great ascetic power.

The divine one has day and night for his eyes, the Vedāṅgas and the Śruti for his ornaments, clarified butter for his nose, the sacrificial ladle for his beak, and the sound of the Sāmaveda chants for his great voice. Vi_1.4.
He consists of the truth of the Dharma, is glorious, and is honored by his successive strides;
he has the great snout of expiation, knees like those of a sacrificial animal, and a magnificent form.
The Udgātṛ priest is its intestines; it has the oblation as its characteristic mark; the seeds and medicinal herbs are its great fruit;
the altar is its inner self; the mantra is its buttocks; and Soma is its blood. Vi_1.6 //
The altar was his shoulder; the sacrificial oblation was his fragrance; he possessed the momentum of offerings to gods and ancestors;
the eastern shed was his body; he was radiant and endowed with various initiations.
The Great One, whose heart is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), consists of the great mantra of Yoga;
his beautiful lips are the *upākarma* ceremony, and he is adorned with the whirlpools of the *pravargya* rite.
His path of movement through various meters, seated upon the secret Upanishads,
accompanied by his shadow-like wife, he indeed rose up like the peak of a jewel-mountain.
The Lord, having entered the single ocean, beheld the earth— bounded by the sea and including its mountains, groves, and forests—
submerged in the waters of that single ocean.
Having lifted it up with the tip of his tusk out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
the Primordial God, the Great Yogi, fashioned the earth anew.
Thus, in ancient times, having assumed the form of the Sacrificial Boar, he who seeks the welfare of all beings raised up the goddess Earth when she had sunk into the subterranean realm of Rasātala.
Having extracted them and established them in their own respective places where they were motionless,
Madhusūdana divided the waters situated therein according to their proper locations.
Those born of the ocean were in the oceans, those born of rivers were in the rivers,
those born of ponds were in the ponds, and those born of lakes were in the lakes.
He created the seven netherworlds (pātāla) as well as the seven worlds (loka),
and the various locations of the continents and the oceans.
The guardians of the quarters, the world-protectors, the rivers, the mountains and forest trees,
the seven sages who know the Dharma, the Vedas with their auxiliary branches, and the gods and asuras.
Piśācas, uragas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and humans;
beasts, birds, wild animals, and the fourfold collection of living beings;
as well as clouds, rainbows, lightning, and various kinds of sacrifices.
Having thus created this world with all its moving and non-moving beings, the Blessed Lord Varāha then departed for a destination unknown to the worlds.
When Janārdana, the god of gods, had departed for an unknown destination, the Earth reflected: "What support will there be for me?"
"I shall go and ask Kaśyapa; he will undoubtedly tell me [the answer], for that great sage constantly bears my concern in mind. (Vi 1.20)
Having thus made her resolve, the goddess, assuming the form of a woman,
went to see Kaśyapa, and Kaśyapa beheld her.
Her eyes were like the petals of a blue lotus, her face resembled the autumnal moon, her hair was adorned with swarms of bees, and she was radiant, with lips as beautiful as the bandhujīva flower.
She had beautiful eyebrows, very fine teeth, a lovely nose, and arched brows;
she possessed a neck like a conch shell, well-knit thighs, and full, rounded hips and thighs.
Her breasts shone forth—symmetrical, full, and close together;
resembling the frontal lobes of Indra’s elephant and possessing a luster like that of refined gold.
His arms were as tender as lotus stalks, his hands like young sprouts,
his thighs resembled pillars of gold, and his knees were well-concealed and closely set.
Her shanks were hairless and perfectly symmetrical, her feet exceedingly beautiful,
and her hips broad, while her waist was like that of a lion cub.
Her copper-colored nails were endowed with radiance, her form was captivating to all,
and she constantly made the quarters of the sky appear filled with blue lotuses by means of her glances.
The goddess, making the quarters free from darkness with her radiance,
was clad in very fine white garments and adorned with the most excellent jewels.
Making the earth appear as if covered with lotuses by her footsteps,
she was endowed with beauty and youth, yet stood before him with humble demeanor.
Seeing her approach and having honored her, Kaśyapa said to that beautiful woman: "O lady of excellent hips, what is in your heart has been understood by me."
"O large-eyed one, hold this fast; go, O Goddess, to Janārdana. He will tell you everything regarding how your steadfastness shall come to pass, O noble lady."
O fair-faced one, O lovely-limbed one, I have learned through the practice of meditation and by his grace that he dwells in the Ocean of Milk for your sake.
Having spoken thus and honored Kaśyapa,
the Earth then departed for the Ocean of Milk, the sea of Keśava, in order to see him.
She beheld that treasury of nectar, enchanting with the rays of the moon,
and agitated by hundreds of waves produced by the agitation of the wind.
Resembling a hundred Himalayas, like another circle of the earth,
it seemed to beckon the land with its moving hands of waves.
By those very rays, he seemed to bestow whiteness upon the moon incessantly;
with all impurities entirely removed by Hari dwelling within him.
Therefore, he bore a body that was exceedingly bright,
powerful, pale-white, capable of traveling through the air, and dwelling in the subterranean realm.
Rich with dark-blue sapphires and tawny gems, it was like the sky turned upside down;
it was as if covered by a multitude of forests brought forth by rows of fruit.
Indeed, seeing that [palace] situated there in the middle, with its exceedingly vast interior like the slough of the serpent Śeṣa, he beheld the abode of Keśava.
Upon that [couch], he beheld Madhusūdana, whose dimensions are indescribable, who is endowed with inconceivable supernatural power, and who was reclining on his side.
His lotus-face was difficult to discern due to the rays from the jewels on the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa;
it resembled a hundred moons and possessed a radiance equal to ten thousand suns.
Akṣobhya, clad in yellow garments and adorned with all kinds of jewels,
is resplendent with a crown the color of the sun and two earrings.
His pair of feet were being massaged by the auspicious palms of Lakṣmī,
while he was being attended on all sides by personified weapons.
Seeing that lotus-eyed Madhusūdana, he prostrated before him,
touching the earth with his knees, and then made this request:
"O Lord Viṣṇu, I who had gone to the depths of the netherworld have been lifted up by you and established in my own place out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds."
"In this matter, O Lord of Gods, what consolation will there now be for me?
When she had spoken thus, the God addressed these words to the Goddess:
O Earth, the virtuous who delight in the conduct of their castes and stages of life and are solely devoted to the scriptures will support you; upon them your burden has been placed.
Thus addressed, Vasumatī spoke to the God of gods:
"O Eternal One, tell me the duties of the social classes and the stages of life."
I wish to hear from you, for you are my supreme refuge;
salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, destroyer of the strength of the enemies of the gods!
O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the World, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace;
O Padmanābha, Hṛṣīkeśa, you of great strength and prowess!
O you who transcend the senses, O most difficult to cross over, O God who wields the Śārṅga bow, O Varāha, O Bhīma, O Govinda, O Ancient One, O Supreme Person! Vi_1.51 //
O golden-haired one, O all-seeing one, O embodiment of sacrifice, O stainless one;
O Lord of the field and the knower of the field, O God, O you who recline upon the ocean of waters! Vi_1.52.
O Mantra, O inconceivable bearer of mantras, whose body is the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
O you who effect the creation and destruction of this entire world! Vi_1.53.
O Knower of Dharma and Adharma, O Limb of Dharma, O Source of Dharma, O Bestower of Boons;
O Viṣvaksena, O Nectar, O Space, O Slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha!
O Great One, known for providing nourishment; O All-pervading One, bestower of fearlessness upon all;
O Most Excellent One, sinless one; O Cloud-like One, creator of the universe! Vi_1.55 //
O nourisher of the waters, abode of the waters, support of consciousness, actionless one;
O teacher of the seven-headed sacrifice, O ancient Supreme Person! Vi_1.56.
O Lord of the eternal syllable, most subtle Master, compassionate toward devotees, and purifier;
You are the refuge of all the gods, and You are the refuge of those who discourse on Brahman.
O Supreme Person, you are the goal of those who have known what is to be known;
O Lord of the World, I have taken refuge in you, the eternal Master, the Lord of Speech.
To Subrahmaṇya, the unassailable, the son of Vasu, the bestower of wealth,
endowed with the power of great yoga, the one born from Pṛśni, who maintains the radiant flame.
To the high-souled Vāsudeva, the lotus-eyed, the infallible,
the god who is the teacher of gods and asuras, the all-pervading Lord, the Great Sovereign of all beings.
O Blessed One, tell me of the single manifestation with four arms, the cause of the cause of the world, and the eternal dharmas for the four castes.
"Endowed with the conduct of the stages of life (āśrama), together with their secret doctrines and their compendiums"—
having been addressed thus by the Earth, the Lord of Gods spoke to the Earth.
Listen, O Goddess Earth, to the eternal duties of the four castes,
together with the conduct of the stages of life, along with their secret doctrines and their essential summaries.
O lady of beautiful thighs, sit upon this excellent golden seat, for you are the supreme refuge for those virtuous ones who shall uphold you.
"Seated comfortably, understand the duties as I proclaim them to you.
At that time, the Earth, seated comfortably, heard the Vaiṣṇava duties. The four social classes (varṇas) are the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Among them, the first three are the twice-born.
For them, the entire collection of rites, beginning with the impregnation ceremony and ending with the funeral at the cemetery, is to be performed according to the mantras.
And their dharmas are as follows.
Teaching the Veda to a Brāhmaṇa. // Vi_2.5 //
For a Kṣatriya, there is constant devotion to weapons.
For the Vaiśya, the tending of cattle.
The duty of the Śūdra is service to the twice-born.
For the twice-born, [the duties are] sacrificing and studying.
Now, their functions are as follows: Vi_2.10.
For a Brāhmaṇa, officiating at sacrifices and receiving gifts [are lawful means of livelihood].
The duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of the earth.
Agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade, money-lending, and the breeding of livestock are the duties of a Vaiśya.
For a Śūdra, all crafts [are lawful].
In times of distress, the immediate livelihood is permitted.
Forbearance, truthfulness, self-restraint, purity, generosity, control of the senses, non-violence, service to the guru, visiting sacred fords, and compassion. Vi_2.16.
Uprightness, freedom from greed, worship of the gods and Brahmins, and likewise freedom from malice—this is called the common dharma. Now, the duties of kings. 3.1.
The protection of the subjects.
The establishment of the social classes and stages of life each in their own respective duty.
And the king should take refuge in a region that is arid, suitable for cattle, and endowed with crops.
And it shall consist mostly of Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
In that regard, one should take refuge in one of the following types of fortresses: those consisting of deserts, marshes, water, trees, or mountains.
And remaining there, he should appoint the local chiefs over their respective villages.
And ten superintendents.
[He should appoint] supervisors over a hundred.
And [he should appoint] provincial governors. Vi_3.10.
The village headman shall provide a remedy for the faults of the village.
If he is unable, he should report it to the superintendent of ten villages.
He too, being unable [to do so], [should report it] to the superintendent of a hundred.
If he too is unable, [he should report it] to the district governor.
Even the ruler of a region should, with his whole being, eradicate evil.
He should appoint trustworthy persons to oversee mines, tolls, ferries, elephants, and forests.
Those who are most righteous in matters of dharma.
They are skillful in matters of purpose and action.
[He sees] heroes in the acts of battle.
The fierce ones among the fierce.
[One should not have sexual intercourse] with eunuchs among women. // Vi_3.21 //
For the sake of tribute from the subjects, he should take a sixth part of the grain produced each year.
And from all grain. // Vi_3.23 //
Two hundred [paṇas] for animals, gold, and garments.
From meat, honey, clarified butter, medicinal herbs, perfumes, flowers, roots, fruits, juices, wood, leaves, skins, earthenware, stone vessels, and wickerwork, the king shall take a sixth part.
One should not collect taxes from Brahmins.
For they are the ones who bring about the Dharma for the king.
And the king receives a sixth part of the merits and demerits of his subjects.
And from goods produced in his own country, he shall take a tenth part as toll.
And from foreign merchandise, one-twentieth [shall be taken].
If he departs from the toll-station, he shall incur the forfeiture of his entire property.
Artisans and those who live by manual labor shall perform one day's work for the king every month.
The sovereign, the ministers, the fortresses, the treasury, the army, the realm, and the allies are the constituent elements of the state.
And he should put to death those who defame him.
And he should have the eye of spies over both his own kingdom and the kingdoms of others.
One should perform the honoring of the virtuous.
And he should put to death those who are wicked.
One should employ conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, and force against enemies, friends, neutrals, and those in between, as is appropriate and according to the time.
And he should resort, as the occasion demands, to peace, war, marching, halting, seeking refuge, or the dual policy.
One should undertake the journey either in the month of Caitra or in Mārgaśīrṣa.
Or when another is in distress. // Vi_3.41 //
Upon arriving in a foreign land, one should not abandon the customs of that country.
And when attacked by an enemy, he should protect his own kingdom with his whole soul.
For kings, there is no dharma equal to the sacrifice of one's body in battle.
Those who are killed while protecting cows, Brahmins, kings, friends, wealth, wives, or their own lives, partake in the heavenly world.
And for the sake of protecting against the intermixture of castes.
Upon the conquest of another's city, the king should consecrate one born of that family there.
One should not destroy a royal family. Vi_3.48.
Except for a royal family of low birth.
One should avoid addiction to hunting, gambling, women, and drinking.
And [the same applies] to verbal abuse and physical assault.
One should not commit an offense against the meaning.
One should not cut off the primary gateways.
One should not rain [one's gifts] upon an unworthy recipient.
One should take everything from mines.
Having found a treasure, he should give half of it to the Brāhmaṇas.
One should cause the second half to enter the treasury.
A Brahmin, having found a treasure-trove, may take it all for himself.
A Kṣatriya should give a fourth part to the king,
a fourth part to the Brāhmaṇas, and take half for himself.
A Vaiśya, however, should give a fourth part to the king,
half to the Brāhmaṇas, and take a fourth part for himself.
And a Śūdra, having divided what he has acquired into twelve parts, shall give five shares to the king,
five shares to the Brāhmaṇas,
and take two shares for himself.
One should confiscate everything from one who has consumed food without first offering it and without having informed [the teacher].
Except for Brāhmaṇas, they shall give a twelfth part of what was deposited by themselves to the king.
One who claims that what was deposited by another was deposited by oneself shall incur a fine equal to that amount.
The king should protect the property of minors, of those without a protector, and of women.
Having recovered wealth stolen by thieves, he should give it all back to those of every social class from whom it was taken.
And if he cannot obtain it from elsewhere, he should give it from his own treasury.
One should pacify the afflictions caused by fate through the means of propitiatory rites and auspicious ceremonies.
And there will be destructions by enemy armies due to the constant presence of weapons.

One should choose as a domestic priest (purohita) a man of noble birth, free from physical defects, devoted to asceticism, and skilled in the meaning of the Vedas, the Itihāsas, and the Dharmaśāstras.
[He should appoint] companions who are pure, free from greed, attentive, and endowed with capability in all matters.
He himself should preside over legal proceedings together with learned Brāhmaṇas.
When presiding over legal proceedings, he should appoint either a Brāhmaṇa.
The king should appoint as members of his assembly those who are endowed with noble birth, proper conduct, and the observance of vows; who are impartial toward both enemy and friend;
and who cannot be subverted by desire, anger, fear, greed, or the pursuit of personal gain.
And the king shall be dependent upon the astrologer in all his affairs.
One should constantly worship the gods and the Brahmins.
One should be a servant of the elders.
And one who performs sacrifices. Vi_3.78.
And within his domain, no Brahmin shall perish from hunger.
Nor is there anyone else devoted to virtuous deeds.
And one should bestow land upon the Brāhmaṇas.

And to those to whom he should grant it— his own kinsmen— he should give a document inscribed on cloth or a copper plate, detailing the extent of the land and the description of the boundaries of the gift, and marked with his own seal, for the information of future kings.
And one should not seize land that has been granted by another.
One should always bestow all gifts upon the Brahmins.
But one should protect oneself from all sides.
And it should be beautiful to behold.
And he is one who maintains the mantras for antidotes that destroy poison.
One should not consume anything that has not been examined.
One should speak with a smile preceded by a gentle greeting.
One should not even frown at those who deserve to be executed.
And he should cause punishment to be inflicted upon those deserving of it, in proportion to their offense.
One should administer punishment correctly.
He would not forgive anyone for a second offense.
For kings, there is no one who does not deserve punishment if they fail to protect their own duty.
Where the dark-complexioned, red-eyed Danda moves about fearlessly,
there the subjects flourish, provided that the leader perceives rightly.
Within his own kingdom, he should administer justice through punishment; he should be severe in punishing enemies;
straightforward toward friends; and endowed with forbearance toward Brahmins.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning grains,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water.

The king who finds happiness in the happiness of his subjects and who is pained by their suffering is endowed with fame in this world and is glorified in heaven after death. A particle of dust situated in a sunbeam passing through a lattice window is known as a *trasareṇu*.
Eight of those [translucent particles] make one nit (likṣā).
Three of those constitute a rājasarṣapa.
Three of those make one white mustard seed (*gaurasarṣapa*).
Six of those [mustis] make one barleycorn (yava).
Three of those [rattis] constitute one *kṛṣṇala*.
Five of those [rathikas] make one māṣa.
That [twelvefold set] is half of an akṣa.
A *suvarṇa* consists of exactly half an *akṣa* plus four *māṣakas*.
A *niṣka* consists of four *suvarṇas*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together constitute one silver *māṣaka*.
Sixteen of those make one dharaṇa.
A copper *kārṣika* is a *kārṣāpaṇa*.
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first *sāhasa* fine;
five hundred are to be known as the middle, and one thousand is the highest. Now, with the exception of Brāhmaṇas, all those who have committed mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) are to be put to death.
There shall be no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa.
He shall banish from his own country a Brāhmaṇa who has been branded with a mark.
And for that [offense], one should fashion a headless human figure upon the forehead as a mark for the killing of a Brahmin.
A tavern sign for drinking liquor. // Vi_5.5 //
For stealing [a dog], one shall become a jackal.
The female organ for sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife. Vi_5.7 //
Even in other cases involving capital punishment, he should banish one who possesses full wealth and remains unhurt.
And the king shall put to death those who forge official edicts.
And those who forge documents. // Vi_5.10 //
Poisoners, arsonists, irresistible thieves, and those who kill women, children, or men.
And those who would steal more than ten jars of grain.
More than a hundred measures of what is to be weighed.
And those who are of low birth who might desire the kingdom.
And those who destroy bridges.
And those who forcibly provide shelter or food to thieves.
Except in the case of the king's inability [to provide protection]. // Vi_5.17 //
A woman whose husband is incapable [of providing for her], and one who has transgressed him. // Vi_5.18 //
If a person of inferior caste commits an offense against one of superior caste with a particular limb, that very limb of his shall be cut off.
One who sits on a single seat with a mark made upon his hip shall be banished.
One should spit and then remove both lips.
And he is one who cannot be intimidated and is devoid of a private part.
And one who reviles is one whose tongue is perverted.
The king should pour boiling oil into the mouths of those who, out of pride, give instructions on the Dharma.
And if one mentions another's name or caste with malice, a ten-finger-long wooden stake shall be driven into his body.
One who speaks falsely regarding what has been heard, one's country, caste, or occupation, shall be fined two hundred kārśāpaṇas.
Even one who speaks the truth regarding those who are one-eyed, lame, and so forth, [is fined] two kārṣāpaṇas. (Vi 5.27)
One who insults his gurus shall pay two hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
But if one brings a charge of a downfall against another, the highest amercement shall be imposed.
For one who has committed a minor offense (upapātaka), the middle [penance] is prescribed.
In the case of reviling those advanced in the three Vedas and in the assemblies of [other] castes. // Vi_5.31 //
And for [the theft of] a village or a district, the first amercement shall be imposed.
For a derisive remark accompanied by a gesture of contempt, the fine is one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
But when it is conjoined with the mother [syllable], it is the highest.
For insulting someone of equal status, one shall be fined twelve paṇas.
For reviling one of inferior appearance or caste, there are six [days of penance].
For the insult of a person of superior caste at an appropriate time, the punishment shall be equal to that [of the preceding offense].
Or three kārṣāpaṇas. // Vi_5.38 //
But in the case of speaking words that are false, it is exactly the same.
But one who has sexual intercourse with the wife of another shall be punished with the highest amercement if she is of the same caste.
In approaching a woman of inferior caste, the middle [offense] applies.
And in sexual intercourse. // Vi_5.42 //
He who approaches a woman of the lowest caste deserves the death penalty.
For approaching a female animal, one shall be fined one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
And one who gives away a maiden without declaring her defects.
And he should maintain her.
One who declares an innocent woman to be guilty shall be punished with the highest amercement.
One who kills an elephant, a horse, a camel, or a cow should be made one-handed and one-footed.
And one who sells meat. // Vi_5.49 //
One who slaughters domestic animals shall be fined one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
He shall pay its value to the owner of the animal.
One who slaughters a wild animal shall pay fifty kārṣāpaṇas.
A bird-killer and a fisherman shall pay ten kārṣāpaṇas.
And for destroying insects, one kārṣāpaṇa.
But one who cuts down a tree that bears fruit commits the highest amercement.
One who cuts down trees that provide flowers incurs the medium [offense].
One who cuts creepers, shrubs, or climbing vines shall pay a fine of one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
One [is the sin of] cutting grass. Vi_5.58.
And all [beings] experience that arising for their respective owners.
He shall quickly be made to pay a fine of ten kārṣāpaṇas.
With the foot, twenty [strokes]. // Vi_5.61 //
For striking with a wooden object, the first amercement shall be imposed.
With a stone, it is middling. // Vi_5.63 //
The highest [merit] is through the sword. Vi_5.64.
For pulling at the feet, hair, garment, or hand, the fine shall be ten paṇas.
One who causes pain without drawing blood shall be fined thirty-two paṇas.
Along with blood, sixty-four [sins].
In the case of breaking a hand, a foot, or a tooth, or of cutting off an ear or the nose, the middle [amercement] applies.
In the obstruction of movement, eating, or speech, and in the inflicting of a blow. // Vi_5.69 //
And [the wound] on the eyes, neck, arms, thighs, or shoulders is of the highest [degree]. Vi_5.70.
The king shall not release from bondage for as long as he lives one who pierces both eyes.
Or one should make it exactly like that.
When many people strike one person, the punishment for each individual shall be double that which was prescribed above.
Of those standing nearby who were not rushing toward him as he cried out, and of those wandering about.
And all those who cause injury to a person shall pay the expenses arising from that injury.
And those who cause suffering to domestic animals. // Vi_5.76 //
One should represent him as having one hand and one foot, and as being carried away by a cow, a horse, a camel, and an elephant.
He is one who does not steal goats or sheep, and he is single-handed.
One who steals grain shall be fined eleven times its value.
And one who steals grain. // Vi_5.80 //
One who steals more than fifty measures of gold, silver, or cloth commits a *vikara* offense.
One who steals less than that shall be fined eleven times the value.

One who steals articles made of thread, cotton, cow-dung, molasses, curd, milk, buttermilk, grass, salt, clay, ashes, birds, fish, ghee, oil, meat, honey, bamboo, cane, earthenware, or metal vessels shall be fined three times their value.
And of cooked foods. // Vi_5.84 //
For the theft of flowers, green shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, or leaves, the fine is five *kṛṣṇalas*.
And [the same applies] to vegetables, roots, and fruits.
One who steals gems shall be punished with the highest amercement.
One who steals articles not previously mentioned shall pay a fine equal to their value.
Thieves shall be made to restore everything stolen to the owner.
Then, the application of the prescribed punishment shall be carried out against them.
He who gives way to those to whom it must be given shall be fined twenty-five kārṣāpaṇas.
And he offered a seat to him who was worthy of a seat.
And they failed to honor those worthy of honor. // Vi_5.93 //
And also for neglecting to invite a neighboring Brahmin. // Vi_5.94 //
And having invited those who bring food. // Vi_5.95 //
Having been invited, they said "So be it," yet they did not eat even a single gold māṣaka.
And one should provide double the amount of food for the one who provides the dwelling.
One who defiles a Brāhmaṇa with forbidden food shall pay a fine of sixteen suvarṇas.
For stealing a person of noble birth, the fine is one hundred [paṇas].
One who drinks liquor is to be executed.
For defiling a Kṣatriya, half of that [penance].
For defiling a Vaiśya, half of that [penance] as well.
For one who defames a Śūdra, the first amercement shall be imposed.
One who is untouchable, by intentionally touching a member of the three higher castes who is touchable, deserves death.
One should strike a woman in her menses with whips.
One who commits an act of impurity even near a path, a garden, or water shall be fined one hundred paṇas.
And one should abandon that as well. Vi_5.107.
One who breaks the ground, walls, or other structures of a house shall be punished with the middle amercement.

Having killed any one of these—a swan, a crane, a balākā, a water-fowl, a monkey, a hawk, a vulture, or a cakravāka—he should give a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a snake, one should give a hoe made of black iron.
Having killed a eunuch, [one receives the fruit of] a load of straw.
Having killed a boar, one obtains a jar of clarified butter.
A partridge [is the price for] a drona of sesame seeds.
A parrot [is equal to] a two-year-old calf.
A three-year-old krauñca bird.
Upon killing a carnivorous beast, one should give a milch cow.
For killing a non-carnivorous wild animal, [the penance is] a heifer.
For killing an animal not specifically mentioned, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
Upon killing a bird, one should eat only at night.
Or he should give a silver māṣa.
Having killed an aquatic creature, one should observe a fast.
But for the killing of a thousand vertebrate creatures,
or for a full cartload of boneless creatures, one should perform the penance prescribed for the murder of a Śūdra.
For killing animals with bones, one should give something small to a Brahmin;
for injuring those without bones, one is purified by a breath-control exercise (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred Ṛg-verses should be recited;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
For all beings born from food, born from moisture,
and those arising from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter is the complete purification.
For the unauthorized cutting of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on a milk-vow.
A drinker of *surā* liquor, excluded from all ritual acts, shall eat only grain-particles for one year.
If one consumes any of the impure intoxicants or alcoholic liquors, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
And [the same applies] to eating garlic, onions, leeks, things having a similar odor, village pigs, village cocks, monkeys, or beef.
In all these cases, at the conclusion of the penance, one should perform the sacramental rite again for the twice-born.
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—these are to be avoided in the rite of re-consecration.
If one eats the meat of five-toed animals, with the exception of the hare, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise, one should fast for seven nights.
Having eaten the food of a member of a religious assembly, a courtesan, a thief, or a singer, one should subsist on milk for seven nights.
The food of a carpenter and of a leather-worker [is forbidden].
And [the water] of usurers, misers, those initiated for a sacrifice, those bound in fetters, those accused of crimes, and eunuchs [is not to be used].
And [one should not eat] the food of unchaste women, hypocrites, physicians, hunters, cruel people, fierce people, and those who eat the leavings of others.
And [the food] of a woman whose husband is not a hero, a goldsmith, a rival wife, and those who have fallen from their status.
And [the sin] of those who speak slander and lies, those who have violated the dharma, and those who sell their own bodies for pleasure.
And [the same applies] to actors, weavers, ungrateful persons, and washermen.
And [the same applies] for those who perform manual labor, those who sit at the feet of others (servants), actors on the stage, lute players, and sellers of weapons.
And [one should avoid] those who live by dogs, those who are addicted to liquor, oil-pressers, weavers, and washermen.
And [the same applies] to those who enter the house of a woman in her menses or of one who has recently given birth.
Food looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a woman in her courses, pecked at by a bird, touched by a dog, or smelled by a cow.
If it is intentionally touched with the foot or sneezed upon. 51.18.
And [it is not an offense] for those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted by illness. // Vi_51.19 //
Meat that has not been honored and meat obtained in vain.
If one eats the flesh of any fish except for the *pāṭhīna*, *rohitaka*, *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and *śakula* species, one should fast for three nights.
And [there is a downfall] for eating the flesh of any aquatic creature. // Vi_51.22 //
Having drunk water that has been kept in a vessel for liquor, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for seven nights.
And those who have stayed in a vessel for liquor [become pure] after five nights.
Having smelled the breath of a liquor-drinker, a soma-drinker shall immerse himself in water, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and then consume clarified butter.
For eating the flesh of a donkey, a camel, or a crow, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having consumed unknown meat from a slaughterhouse, or dried meat. 51.27.
For eating the flesh of carnivorous beasts or birds, one must perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
If one eats the flesh of the kalaviṅka, plava, cakravāka, haṃsa, rajjudāla, sārasa, dātyūha, śuka, sārikā, baka, balākā, kokila, or khañjarīṭa, one should fast for three nights.
And [the same applies] to eating the flesh of single-hoofed animals and those with teeth in both jaws.
And for eating the flesh of any bird, with the exception of the partridge, the grey partridge, the common quail, the francolin, and the peacock, there is a fast of one day and night.
Having eaten insects for one day, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*.
And [there is a downfall] for eating the flesh of dogs. // Vi_51.33 //
For eating mushrooms and fungi, one must perform the Sāntapana penance.
Having avoided preparations of barley, wheat, and milk, as well as fatty substances, fermented liquids, and *khāṇḍava* sweets, one should fast after consuming whatever has become stale.
And tree-exudations that arise from incisions or are impure, as well as those that are red.
The lotus-root, rice cooked with meat, kṛsara, saṃyāva, milk-rice, cakes, fried pastries, food intended for the gods, and sacrificial oblations; // Vi_51.37 //
And all other milks, with the exception of those from cows, goats, and buffaloes.
And those [days] as well, if they are less than ten days.
And the milk of a cow that flows [excessively], one that is pregnant, or one whose calf has died. // Vi_51.40 //
And those who eat impure substances. // Vi_51.41 //
And those that have turned sour, with the exception of curd.
One who is in the stage of student celibacy (brahmacaryāśramin) shall fast for three nights after eating at a funeral feast (śrāddha).
And he should dwell in water for one day.
For eating honey or meat, one must perform the Prājāpatya penance.
If one eats the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mongoose, or a rat, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*.
Having eaten the leavings of another on the day before, one should fast for one day and drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For eating the excrement or urine of five-toed animals, [the penance lasts] seven nights.
If one eats at a funeral rite for a raw corpse (āmaśrāddha), one should subsist on milk alone for three nights.
A Brāhmaṇa who eats the leavings of a Śūdra must fast for seven nights.
For eating the remnants of a Vaiśya's meal, [one must fast] for five nights.
If one eats the leavings of a Kṣatriya, the penance lasts for three nights.
But for eating the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa, the penance is one day.
A Kṣatriya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra shall fast for five nights.
One who eats the remnants of a Vaiśya's meal shall fast for three nights.
A Vaiśya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra [is likewise excluded].
Having eaten the food of a Caṇḍāla, one should fast for three nights.
Having eaten prepared food, one must perform the Parāka penance.
A Brahmin should never eat animals that have not been consecrated with mantras;
however, abiding by the eternal rule, he may eat those consecrated with mantras.
As many hairs as there are on the animal's body, for that many times does the slaughterer undergo death here;
thus the killer of animals receives no atonement either in this world or after passing away.
"Beasts were created by the Self-Existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
for sacrifice leads to the prosperity of all. Therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not killing."
The sin of a hunter seeking wealth does not become as great as that which accrues after death to one who eats meat in vain.
Herbs, animals, trees, crawling creatures, and likewise birds,
having met their death for the sake of sacrifice, attain higher states once again.
In the honey-mixture offering, in sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors and the gods—
only in these instances may animals be slain, and never under any other circumstances.
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas, by killing animals for the sake of sacrifice,
leads both himself and those animals to the highest state.
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Vedas, even in times of distress.
One should know that the violence ordained by the Vedas, which is restricted to this world of moving and non-moving beings, is indeed non-violence; for dharma has shone forth from the Veda.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, neither while living nor even when dead.
He who does not desire to inflict upon living beings the afflictions of bondage and slaughter,
seeking the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness.
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one does, and wherever one fixes one's attachment—
to that very thing one attains without effort, provided one harms nothing at all.
Meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the killing of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat.
Having carefully considered the origin of meat and the slaughter and imprisonment of embodied beings, one should desist from eating all kinds of meat.
He who does not eat meat, even when following the prescribed rule, like a *piśāca*,
becomes beloved in the world and is not afflicted by diseases.
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and seller,
the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it— all these are slayers.
There is no doer of unmeritorious deeds greater than he who, without having honored the ancestors and the gods, desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another.
He who might perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years,
and he who does not eat meat— the merit and fruit of these two are equal.
One does not obtain that fruit by consuming divine fruits and roots, nor by eating the food of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat.
"He who eats my flesh here shall eat me in the next world;

One who has committed the theft of gold, confessing his deed to the king, should offer a wooden pestle.

And one who steals grain or wealth must perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year.

For those [who have consumed] food, drink, vehicles, beds, seats, flowers, roots, or fruits, there is the drinking of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

For stealing gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver, iron, or bell-metal, one should eat only grain-particles for twelve days.
For stealing cotton, silk, wool, and so forth, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
Upon stealing animals with cloven hooves or solid-hooved animals, one should fast for two nights.
For stealing birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, ropes, or articles made of split bamboo, one should fast for a day.
Having recovered the property that was taken after having been given, even from the creditor by some means,

Whatever a man who is unrestrained might take from others,
by that very thing he shall be deprived whenever he is reborn.
Since both life and the desire for the Dharma are established upon wealth,

He who is intent on harming living beings and likewise he who is intent on harming wealth—
of these two, the one intent on harming wealth encounters great suffering.

Now, regarding approaching a woman who should not be approached, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance for a year in the forest, wearing garments of bark according to the procedure for the Great Vow (mahāvrata).

A member of the royal caste [should wait] for two days.

A Śūdra [should eat] at night.

If he approaches his wife during her season except on the forbidden lunar days, he shall fast for three nights.
A false witness shall perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Brahmin.
If one voids urine or feces in a place lacking water, one must bathe with one's clothes on and perform the Mahāvyāhṛti oblation.
One who has been released from the offense of sleeping while the sun is rising shall bathe with his clothes on and repeat the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred and eight times.

An atheist, one who lives like an atheist, an ungrateful person, a fraudulent dealer, and one who destroys the livelihood of Brahmins—these shall subsist on alms for one year.

And one should further lead him toward that [state].
Having traveled by camel or donkey, or having bathed naked, slept, or eaten, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Having recited the Sāvitrī three thousand times with a concentrated mind,

Having performed sacrifices for those unworthy of sacrificing, having performed funeral rites for others, and having practiced malevolent magic or the Ahīna sacrifice, one removes that sin by means of three Kṛcchra penances.

One should not have any dealings with those who have been purified from sin;

One who has restrained the breath should recite three times the Gāyatrī together with the Vyahṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras; that is called prāṇāyāma.

The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*,
together with the three-footed *Gāyatrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
He who studies this day after day for three years without sloth reaches the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and possessing a form of space.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity;
there is nothing higher than the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence.
All Vedic rites of oblation and sacrifice flow away;
however, the Imperishable should be known as the Imperishable, as well as Brahmā and Prajāpati.

The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the ritual sacrifice (vidhiyajña). The whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is said to be a hundredfold more effective, and the mental recitation (mānasa) a thousandfold.

Now, those who are to be abandoned: Vi_57.1.

Those who are impure for three generations on both the mother’s and the father’s side [are ineligible].
All of them are indeed unfit to be eaten from and unfit to receive gifts from.
And one should avoid the habit of accepting gifts from those whose gifts are not to be accepted.
Through the acceptance of gifts, the Vedic splendor of Brahmins perishes.
He who accepts a gift without understanding the rules for receiving material objects sinks down together with the giver.
And he who, though capable of accepting gifts, refrains from accepting them, attains the world of the givers.
One should not reject fuel, water, roots, fruits, protection, meat, honey, bedding, seats, houses, flowers, curd, or vegetables when they are offered.
Prajāpati considered that alms offered spontaneously upon being invited, presented before him without prior solicitation, may be accepted even from one of evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years of him who treats that [cow] with contempt, nor does the fire carry his sacrificial oblation.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the ancestors and the gods,
he may accept gifts from all sources, but he should not satisfy himself with them.
Even when capable of receiving these [gifts] for the sake of such duties,
one should not accept them from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, or an enemy.
But when the teachers have passed away, or when living at home without them,
one seeking one's own livelihood should always receive it from a virtuous person.
A partner in a business, a family friend, a slave, a cowherd, and a barber—
these among Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
Now, for one living in the householder stage of life, there are three kinds of wealth.
White, variegated, and black.
Whatever funeral rites he performs with pure wealth, by that he attains divinity.
That which is variegated is human existence.
That which was done by Kṛṣṇa resulted in his birth as an animal.
That which is earned by one's own labor is "white" for everyone.
That which is acquired through immediate succession is variegated.
And that which is acquired through an intermittent mode of activity is black.
Inheritance received in succession, a gift of affection, and property acquired together with one's wife— this wealth is declared to be "pure" (śukla) for all without distinction.
That which is obtained through bribes or taxes, through the sale of what should not be sold,
or received from one who has rendered a service, is declared to be "stained" (śabala) wealth.
That which is acquired through gambling, theft, forgery, violence,
or by means of deception is declared to be "black" wealth.
Whatever a person performs with whatever kind of material substance,
he obtains a corresponding fruit both in this world and after death.
A householder should perform the *pākayajñas* in the nuptial fire.
And one should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice both in the evening and in the morning.
One should offer oblations to the deities. Vi_59.3.
One should sacrifice with the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa offerings at the times of the conjunction and the opposition of the moon and the sun.
The expiation is by means of an animal sacrifice.
And during the autumn and summer, one should perform the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice.
Or [it may be performed] when rice and barley have been cooked.
We have more than enough for three years.
Every year, [he should sacrifice] with the Soma.
In the absence of wealth, [one should perform] the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice.
One should bestow in its entirety all the wealth obtained by begging for the sake of a sacrifice.
One should offer the Vaiśvadeva oblation every evening and morning.
And one should give alms to a monk.
By giving alms to one who has been honored, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow.
In the absence of a monk, one should give even a single mouthful of food to the cows.
Or one should cast it into the fire.
Even when food is already being eaten, one should not turn away a beggar.
The mortar and pestle, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and the broom—these are the five slaughter-houses of the householder.
And for the sake of expiating that, one should perform sacrifices to Brahman, the gods, the spirits, the ancestors, and humans.
The recitation of sacred texts is the sacrifice to Brahman.
A human being is divine.
The libation for the ancestors is that which pertains to the ancestors.
Bali is a Bhūta. Vi_59.23.
The sacrifice to men consists of honoring guests.
He who does not offer sustenance to these five— the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— does not truly live, even though he breathes.
The student, the ascetic, and the mendicant live by means of the householder's stage of life;
therefore, a householder should not treat these guests with contempt.
The householder alone performs sacrifice; the householder practices austerity;
and the householder gives gifts; therefore, the one in the householder stage of life is the best.
The sages, the ancestors, the gods, living beings, and likewise guests, all look for support from householders; therefore, the householder stage of life is the most excellent.
By constantly practicing the pursuit of the three aims of life, giving food, worshipping the gods, honoring Brahmins,
engaging in the study of the Vedas, and offering libations to the ancestors, a householder attains the station of Śakra.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should perform the evacuation of urine and feces.
At night one should face south, during the day one should face north, and at the two twilights one should face east.
Nor on ground that has not been covered. // Vi_60.3 //

Having thus praised her with a serene mind, the goddess Earth, her desire fulfilled, then spoke face-to-face to the Queen.

Having seen the Goddess Śrī, who had taken hold of the feet of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, blazing with ascetic fervor and possessing the beautiful hue of well-refined gold, the Earth, filled with joy, questioned her.
O you who possess hands as beautiful as blooming red lotuses, O most excellent one; O you whose feet are grasped by a navel like a blooming red lotus;
O you who always abide in a dwelling like a blooming red lotus; O you whose complexion is equal to the center of a blooming red lotus.
O you with eyes like blue lotuses, with a complexion like refined gold, clad in white garments, your limbs adorned with jewels;
O moon-faced one, possessing a radiance equal to the sun, of great power, the foremost in the world!
You alone are the primary sleep of the world, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Śrī, Virati, and Jayā;
you are Kānti, Prabhā, Kīrti, and Vibhūti; you are Sarasvatī, Vāk, and Pāvanī.
Svadhā, Titikṣā, Vasudhā, Pratiṣṭhā, Sthiti, Sudīkṣā, as well as Sunīti; Khyāti, Viśālā, Anasūyā, Svāhā, Medhā, and likewise Buddhi.

O dark-eyed one, just as this best of gods stands having pervaded the entire triple world, so too do you stand, O giver of boons; nevertheless, O powerful one, I ask you about the abode of your majesty.
Having been addressed in this way, Lakṣmī, standing before the best of gods, then spoke to the Earth:
"O you of golden hue, I am always stationed at the side of the god Madhusūdana."
"O Sustainer of the World, listen: by his command, the virtuous declare that I am he whom I remember in my mind, endowed with glory; and hear also where I always abide when he is being remembered."
I dwell in the sun and in the moon, in the cloudless sky rich with hosts of stars,
as well as in clouds heavy with rain and flashing with lightning, adorned with Indra’s bow.
Likewise, O Earth, upon pure gold and silver, upon stainless jewels and garments, upon rows of white palaces, and upon temples adorned with banners; ||| Vi_99.10 |||

When cow dung has just been spread, when a lordly elephant is in rut, when a horse is exultant, when a bull is likewise filled with pride, and when a Brahmin is similarly engaged in Vedic study; ||| Vi_99.11 |||

I am likewise situated upon the lion-throne, the *āmalaka* fruit, the *bilva* fruit, the parasol, the conch, and the lotus; in the blazing fire, the stainless sword, and the reflection in the mirror. Vi_99.12.
I stood upon fresh, newly dug earth amidst decorated water-jars filled to the brim, accompanied by fly-whisks and palm-leaf fans, and among charming golden ewers.
Likewise in milk, in clarified butter, in green grass, in honey, and in curd;
in the body of a virtuous housewife, in the body of a maiden, and in the bodies of the gods, of ascetics, and of those who have offered oblations in sacrifice. Vi_99.14.

Whether in an arrow, in one who has emerged victorious from battle, in one standing firm, in one who has died and gone to dwell in heaven, in the sound of the Vedas, in the blast of a conch, in the utterance of *svāhā* and *svadhā*, or in the sound of musical instruments; // Vi_99.15 //
Likewise at a royal consecration, at a wedding, at a sacrifice, or when one has bathed one's head;
among white flowers, on mountains, with delightful fruits, and by the best of rivers.

In lakes full of water, likewise in waters and on ground covered with green grass, in a cluster of lotuses, in the forest, in a calf, in a joyful infant, and in a virtuous man devoted to dharma; // Vi_99.17 //

One who is devoted to proper conduct, constant in the study of the scriptures, modest in dress as well as well-attired, perfectly pure and self-controlled, free from impurity, eating wholesome food, and a worshiper of guests; Vi_99.18.

Content with his own wife and devoted to dharma, he was intensely dedicated to righteousness and free from overeating; always adorned with flowers, his body fragrant and anointed with perfumes, and well-decorated.
Established in truth, intent on the welfare of beings, endowed with patience and free from anger,
skilled in his own affairs and skilled in the affairs of others, he was always of virtuous mind and disciplined.
Among women who are always well-adorned, devoted to their husbands, speaking kindly, not stingy with their hands, blessed with sons, careful in guarding household goods, and fond of making offerings;
I always abide among those women whose dwellings are well-swept, who have conquered their senses, who are free from strife, who are without greed,
who regard righteousness, who are endowed with compassion, and who are ever devoted to Madhusūdana.
And without the Supreme Person, I shall never remain for even a single moment.
This preeminent treatise on Dharma was spoken by the Lord himself;
those twice-born who uphold it shall attain the highest state in heaven.
This is purifying, auspicious, leading to heaven, and indeed bestowing long life;
it is knowledge itself, conferring fame, and increasing wealth and good fortune.
It should be studied, retained, recited, and listened to;
and it should always be made heard by those endowed with faith, by men who desire prosperity.
The man who always desires prosperity and recites this constantly— O Earth,
this supreme secret has been told to you.
With a clear mind, for the sake of the welfare of the world, I have composed this supreme and glorious work,
which destroys bad dreams, is endowed with great merit, is an abode of auspiciousness, and is an eternal treatise on Dharma.
